channel.title: Tea with Ree
channel.description: A space to pause and reflect. Thoughtful writing on wellbeing, nature, inner work and modern life.

item.title: Rest Is Not a Reward | Tea with Ree
item.description: I have treated rest as something I could earn for a long time. Finish the work. Answer the messages. Be useful. Then perhaps there would be a quiet afternoon waiting for me at the end of it all.

item.title: The Life You Keep Beginning | Tea with Ree
item.description: There have been several beginnings in my life. Some were planned. Some arrived because the old way could not continue. I used to think beginning again meant I had failed to settle. Now I think it can mean that I am still listening.

item.title: The Voice You Use With Yourself | Tea with Ree
item.description: I used to think confidence meant speaking loudly enough that nobody could misunderstand me. I know better now. Some of the strongest changes in my life began quietly, with the way I spoke to myself when nobody else could hear.

item.title: The Body Is Not a Project | Tea with Ree
item.description: There are days when movement feels joyful and days when it feels like one more demand. I have learned that both can be true without turning the body into a problem to solve.

item.title: The Future Should Still Have Room for People | Tea with Ree
item.description: I am interested in technology when it brings people into better conversations, not when it tries to make the people unnecessary. A tool can organise a meeting, find a pattern, or help with a first draft. It cannot decide what matters to the people sitting around the table.

item.title: What Responsible AI Means on an Ordinary Day | Tea with Ree
item.description: I have spent the past year working closely with AI tools and I am interested in what they mean beyond the excitement. The important questions are often ordinary ones. What happens to our privacy? Who is responsible when an answer is wrong? Does a useful tool give us time back, or does it quietly take over our judgement?

item.title: A Tool Is Only as Wise as the Question | Tea with Ree
item.description: There is something almost ritual about setting a cup of tea down and looking out at the small rectangle of sky my kitchen window offers. It is an ordinary pause, but it reminds me that tools are best judged by the company they keep. A perfectly good kettle will not warm a cold room and a clever app will not find the answer you need unless you know how to ask it. The way we frame a question sets the direction of everything that follows.

item.title: Can AI Help the Climate Without Becoming Another Cost? | Tea with Ree
item.description: Lately I have been thinking about the neat, clever tools that promise to help us meet climate goals. They can do startling things with data, spot patterns we would otherwise miss and suggest where resources might be stretched further. But as useful as these systems can be, I worry we too easily treat them as a simple fix, rather than as something that needs careful tending.

item.title: Can Technology Help Us Notice More? | Tea with Ree
item.description: I have a small ritual of standing at the kitchen sink for a minute before I turn on the kettle, partly because it feels like an odd kind of permission to just be. Lately I have been aware of how much the tools in my pocket and on my wrist shape that minute and whether they help me notice the things I want to notice.

item.title: The Cost of Convenience | Tea with Ree
item.description: I make a cup of tea, the kettle humming on its own and a notification tells me my shopping will arrive in an hour. There is a small comfort in that certainty. It means no trolley-wrangling in the rain, no rummaging for loose change at the shop counter and no need to plan the day around opening hours. It also nudges a question that sits quietly at the back of my mind: at what point does ease start to cost more than money?

item.title: When a Recommendation Becomes a Narrowing | Tea with Ree
item.description: There is a peculiar economy to suggestions. One small nudge on my screen and the afternoon seems to rearrange itself, as if the app, the playlist or the online shop has quietly decided what I ought to like next.

item.title: The Infrastructure We Forget | Tea with Ree
item.description: I was making a pot of tea the other morning and noticed the kettle click off before I had time to breathe. It felt like a small miracle, which of course it is when you think about the wire and metal and company of engineers that make that single familiar sound possible.

item.title: What I Learnt from Travelling Alone | Tea with Ree
item.description: There is a peculiar kind of quiet the moment you button your coat and walk out by yourself, suitcase in hand.

item.title: The Small Rituals That Make a Day Softer | Tea with Ree
item.description: There is a particular comfort in doing something small and ordinary on purpose.

item.title: When the Old Version of You Calls | Tea with Ree
item.description: Sometimes, late in the evening when the washing-up has been done and there is a mug of tea cooling at my elbow, I hear the old version of me on the line.

item.title: Ageing Without Apology | Tea with Ree
item.description: There is a small, steady pleasure in noticing how my days have shifted shape.

item.title: The Health Advice I No Longer Chase | Tea with Ree
item.description: Health advice arrives daily, bright and certain, offering a neat formula for looking, feeling or performing better.

item.title: The Medicine of a Good Laugh | Tea with Ree
item.description: You know that little alchemy that happens when a laugh breaks out?

item.title: The Wellness Event as a Shared Room | Tea with Ree
item.description: I turned up to a local wellness event the way you might arrive at someone's flat for an evening.

item.title: Thriving Is More Than Feeling Fine | Tea with Ree
item.description: I often think of thriving as a slightly more honest word than happiness.

item.title: What My Garmin Taught Me About Effort | Tea with Ree
item.description: When I first strapped a Garmin to my wrist I expected it to be a strict accountant of exertion.

item.title: What the Body Knows Before the App Does | Tea with Ree
item.description: There is a small, steady voice that lives in the margins of my day. It is not loud, it does not arrive with a notification sound.

item.title: When Technology Has to Explain Itself | Tea with Ree
item.description: I read something this morning that made me put my cup down.

item.title: Abstract Tech: Visual Language of the Future | Tea with Ree
item.description: Technology has developed its own aesthetic. Neon grids. Glitch effects. Holographic interfaces. These visuals are not just decoration. They are a visual language that signals innovation, futurity and the dissolution of boundaries between physical and digital.

item.title: AI as a Creative Companion | Tea with Ree
item.description: I think technology should feel like an extension of what you actually want to do, not a replacement for thinking. The best tools are the ones that get out of your way and let you think more clearly, create more freely and connect more deeply.

item.title: The Rise of Digital Rituals | Tea with Ree
item.description: We think of rituals as ancient. Candles. Chants. Offerings. But the human need for ritual is not bound to any technology. It is bound to intention.

item.title: Building a Second Brain | Tea with Ree
item.description: Your mind is for having ideas, not holding them. That is the idea behind the second brain movement and honestly, it has changed how I think. Externalise your thinking so that your biological brain is free to do what it does best: connect, create and wonder.

item.title: Inside the Sauna | Tea with Ree
item.description: The sauna is a small wooden room that smells of cedar and effort. I've been using it for two years now and I still feel a small thrill every time I open the door. Like I'm about to step into somewhere that demands my full attention.

item.title: Movement as Medicine | Tea with Ree
item.description: The body isn't a machine. It's a landscape. Weather and seasons and terrain that shifts whether you ask it to or not. It has weather and seasons and terrain that changes with use and disuse. Movement is how we tend that landscape.

item.title: Conversations with a Reiki Practitioner | Tea with Ree
item.description: I met Amara at a wellness fair in Johannesburg. Her table was modest. A few crystals. A business card. A calm that seemed to radiate from her skin. I was sceptical. I am still sceptical. But I was also curious.

item.title: Do Wellness Trackers Really Work? | Tea with Ree
item.description: I strapped an Oura Ring to my finger and a Garmin to my wrist and waited for enlightenment. Spoiler: it didn't arrive in a push notification. The devices promised data. Sleep stages. Heart rate variability. Recovery scores. After three months, I had to ask: did I feel any better?

item.title: The Quiet Work of Continuing | Tea with Ree
item.description: There is a version of persistence that looks impressive from a distance. It has clean mornings, strong opinions and a calendar full of evidence that someone is moving forward.

item.title: What a Nervous System Reset Really Means | Tea with Ree
item.description: Your nervous system is basically the body’s alarm and recovery system. It’s constantly scanning for threat or safety. When life piles on deadlines, notifications, arguments, traffic, old stress that never fully left it can get stuck in “on” mode. Heart rate up, muscles tight, mind racing, gut unsettled. That’s the sympathetic side running the show (fight, flight, or freeze).

item.title: Palms Together | Tea with Ree
item.description: Wellbeing is quieter than the routines we’re sold. It’s less about adding things and more about coming back.

item.title: When the Tools Start Using Us | Tea with Ree
item.description: Tools have a funny way of growing beyond their purpose. The answer isn’t to throw the laptop out of the window. It’s to stay the one in charge.

item.title: Adjusting the Lens | Tea with Ree
item.description: We don’t just see the world; we see it through something. Inner work is the slow, honest practice of noticing the lens.

item.title: The Green Behind the Glass | Tea with Ree
item.description: Most of us live with nature in the background. It’s there, but slightly blurred, while we frown at our notebooks and our deadlines.

item.title: What Mentoring Has Taught Me About Advice | Tea with Ree
item.description: Two cups of tea sit on a small table between two chairs. One steam ring has already cooled to a pale bloom on the saucer. We have both been here before, not always with the same names, not always the same questions, but the same human tendency to want a tidy answer handed across the table.

item.title: The Difference Between Assistance and Dependence | Tea with Ree
item.description: My favourite mornings begin with the tactile ritual of shutting my laptop, nudging a notebook towards me and making a single neat line down the margin. The gesture is small and domestic. It is also a test. Closing the laptop does not make the world less clever. What it does is remind me that some decisions need human attention, the sort of attention that cannot be outsourced to the pleasing certainty of a search result or an algorithmic nudge.

item.title: What AI Can Give Back to a Human Day | Tea with Ree
item.description: On the kitchen table this morning my laptop sat beside a sheaf of handwritten notes and a cooling cup of tea. The notes were flecked with scribbles and arrows and the kind of small, useful mistakes that tell you you have been thinking for yourself. The laptop offered a different kind of promise, pages of text waiting to be nudged into shape. I have been learning how to let the two coexist rather than compete. The question I keep returning to is not what AI can do for me but what it can give back to the human parts of my day.

item.title: What My Oura Ring Taught Me About Sleep | Tea with Ree
item.description: There is a small circle of metal I take off the moment I wash my hands and rest on the bedside table beside whatever book I am reading. It is unobtrusive in a way a wristband is not. It feels private and a little companionable. Wearing it has not turned me into a perfect sleeper. What it has done is change how I notice sleep and how quickly I equate a number with either success or failure.

item.title: A Day Without Eating | Tea with Ree
item.description: I used to think fasting was a discipline you performed for someone else to notice. A neat achievement, mentioned once it was safely over.

item.title: Fifth Place and Fine With It | Tea with Ree
item.description: I used to think a step count was just a number competing with other numbers. Now I think it might be one of the more honest measures of a life I have.

item.title: The Run I Hadn't Trained For | Tea with Ree
item.description: I used to think showing up was most of the job. If I turned up willing, I assumed the rest would sort itself out.

item.title: What GLP-1 Actually Means and What My Own Sugar Habit Taught Me | Tea with Ree
item.description: I used to hear GLP-1 mentioned as though it were a brand rather than a hormone, another word in the general noise around weight loss drugs. I want to explain it properly, because I think most people repeating the term have never actually been told what it means.

item.title: The Path Less Travelled | Tea with Ree
item.description: Everyone told me to take the safe road. I did not always listen.

item.title: A Face Is a Design Decision | Tea with Ree
item.description: Warmth is cheap to produce and easy to fake. On the difference between how a tool feels to deal with and whether it can be relied on.

item.title: In the Wrong Element | Tea with Ree
item.description: A penguin on rock looks like a creature managing. On how much of what we call weakness is really the wrong surroundings.

item.title: Whose Hands Hold the Shears | Tea with Ree
item.description: We’re all cultivated by the people around us. On telling the difference between a shape you chose and one you were trained into.

item.title: Where the Earth Breathes | Tea with Ree
item.description: Steam, sulphur and ground that offers us nothing. On a planet that has never once been settled, and doesn’t need our approval.

item.title: A Garden Is a Small Climate Conversation | Tea with Ree
item.description: A patch of garden measurably cools the air around it compared to the pavement nearby, cities have measured this for years. Not everyone gets a garden.

item.title: In Praise of Small Joys | Tea with Ree
item.description: Researchers who study this call it a micro-moment of positivity resonance, a brief instant of shared good feeling between two beings that measurably lifts wellbeing on its own.

item.title: What Blue and Blaze Have Taught Me About Time | Tea with Ree
item.description: Dogs carry something like 300 million scent receptors in their noses, against roughly six million in ours. Blue uses his properly.

item.title: When Love for One Dog Becomes Care for Many | Tea with Ree
item.description: A dog wearing a bandana or a collar in its photo tends to find a home faster than one without, shelters have long since worked that out. A dog waits at an adoption day wearing a red bandana that says ADOPT ME.

item.title: Eco-Tips for Everyday Living | Tea with Ree
item.description: There is more gold in a tonne of discarded circuit boards than in seventeen tonnes of mined ore, sitting in a kitchen drawer waiting to be noticed.

item.title: Oceans in Focus: A Visual Essay | Tea with Ree
item.description: Marine phytoplankton generate something like half of the oxygen we breathe, an entire planet's worth of air moving through water with no edges. Two turtles moving through blue that has no edges.

item.title: Rescue Stories That Restore Hope | Tea with Ree
item.description: It takes about fifteen minutes for a frightened shelter dog's stress hormone levels to measurably drop, once someone simply sits with it.

item.title: From Shelter to Sanctuary: One Dog’s Journey | Tea with Ree
item.description: The shelter smelled of disinfectant and hope. Researchers have a name for what happens next between a dog and the person who stays.

item.title: What Trees Give Us Before We Notice | Tea with Ree
item.description: There's a recognised word, solastalgia, for the specific grief people feel when a landscape they love is suddenly damaged or destroyed.

item.title: Sustainable Living When the Forecast Is a Warning | Tea with Ree
item.description: A single frictionless click is often all it takes to bypass the pause that would normally stop an impulse buy, retailers have known this for years. There's a moment before you order it.

item.title: A Softer Monday | Tea with Ree
item.description: Monday gets a bad name it does not fully deserve.

item.title: Affirmations, Self-Belief and the Stories We Repeat | Tea with Ree
item.description: Affirmations are just you saying stuff to yourself on purpose. “I am enough.” “I can handle this.” “I’m getting better.” That is it.

item.title: Confidence After 40: A Quiet Revolution | Tea with Ree
item.description: There is a particular confidence that arrives after forty. It does not announce itself with trumpets. (I wish it did. I would have noticed sooner.) It slips in through the back door, wearing comfortable shoes and sits down without asking permission.

item.title: The Discipline of Noticing Small Joys | Tea with Ree
item.description: We are trained to notice what is wrong. The missed deadline. The slight insult. That one body part that refuses to behave. This negativity bias served our ancestors well. It kept them alive. But in a world where survival is less urgent, the same bias keeps us miserable.

item.title: Journaling Prompts for Stillness | Tea with Ree
item.description: A journal is not a diary. It is not a record of what happened. It is a laboratory for what might happen if you thought differently. The page is the safest place I know.

item.title: Learning to Fail Without Becoming Smaller | Tea with Ree
item.description: I used to think failure had a sound. It was the silence after an email went unanswered. The pause in a room when I had said too much. The small internal collapse that arrived when a plan I had believed in did not work, even though I had given it my best attention.

item.title: Three-Minute Morning Meditations | Tea with Ree
item.description: You do not need an hour. You do not need a cushion. You do not need to chant in Sanskrit or burn incense. You need three minutes. A chair. And the willingness to stop.

item.title: The Day the Light Stepped Aside | Tea with Ree
item.description: The eclipse is not here. It is in Spain. Today the moon crosses the sun over southern Europe and half the world is travelling to stand beneath it. I am not. I am reading about it from here, the way you read about a wedding you were not invited to but are glad is happening.

item.title: A World Made Smaller by Birds | Tea with Ree
item.description: The Macaw Recovery Network, which works with rescued macaws in Costa Rica, describes allofeeding, mouth to mouth feeding between mates, as one of the behaviours that keeps a pair bonded for life.

item.title: Conservation Begins with Attention | Tea with Ree
item.description: Between one and a half and four million people in India make a living sorting through what everyone else decided was worthless.

item.title: Rainforest After Rain | Tea with Ree
item.description: A single mature canopy tree can lift over a thousand litres of water into the air in a single day, entire forests studies have measured this repeatedly.

item.title: The Air We Share | Tea with Ree
item.description: Roughly 182 million tons of dust lift off the Sahara every year. Only a portion of that, something like 27 million tons, actually completes the crossing to the Amazon, the rest scatters elsewhere over the Atlantic.

item.title: What We Owe the Soil | Tea with Ree
item.description: Underneath a healthy forest floor, a network of fungal threads connects root systems across whole acres, quietly moving carbon, water, and warning signals between trees that share nothing else.

item.title: A Letter to the Woman Still Becoming | Tea with Ree
item.description: I am writing because some afternoons the house is quiet enough for thoughts to land and stay and a quiet kindness feels overdue.

item.title: How to Stay Tender Without Becoming Naive | Tea with Ree
item.description: There is a softness I keep like a favourite mug, easy to reach for and, if I am honest, sometimes at risk of being chipped.

item.title: Learning to Take Up Space Kindly | Tea with Ree
item.description: There is a strange, familiar tug when someone else fills the room with their laugh, their volume, their presence and you find yourself literally shrinking.

item.title: The Courage to Be Seen Learning | Tea with Ree
item.description: Sitting with a warm cup of tea, I often find my thoughts returning to the same awkward, delightful problem.

item.title: The Difference Between Company and Connection | Tea with Ree
item.description: There are times when a room full of people feels like background noise and a single conversation feels like an anchor.
